source.title: Exploring and Developing a Pre-Model Safeguard with Draft Models
source.authors: Hongyu Cai; Arjun Arunasalam; Yi-Ming Liang; Antonio Bianchi; Z. B. Celik

page_placements.theme: Optimized input attacks have conditional transfer and placement effects

record.tranche_reason: Tests transfer of jailbreak attacks to smaller draft models, a new model-size setting; its results also bear on the suffix-attack part of V4.
record.gate_note: The study tests jailbreak prompts generated by GCG, AutoDAN, and PAIR, and reports unsafe responses and transferability. It does not test fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, decoding changes, safety-localizing weight edits, causes of shallowness, or deepening training. Its safeguard DFR and latency results evaluate the proposed guard, not the claim versions, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether jailbreak prompts optimised on large aligned LLMs also make small draft models (OPT-125M-AWQ, SmolLM-135M, etc.) emit unsafe text. It then uses that as a signal for a pre-model guard. Most draft models are base or lightly tuned small models, not safety-trained systems whose refusal is bypassed. No row compares a harmful prompt with and without the attack. The study reports no attack success rate on the aligned target LLMs, and nothing isolates getting past the opening tokens. So no result bears on whether prefills, suffixes or decoding changes defeat refusal (V4) or on any other version. Qi et al. is cited only as an example of training-data poisoning. The cross-model transfer finding is a related construct and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that jailbreaks transfer from LLMs to SLMs, with transfer depending on the model pair, attack method, iterations and intent category. They argue this transfer can serve defence: a draft-model guard cuts defence failure rate by an average of 32.4% versus pre-model guards. Against post-model guards it gives comparable or lower failure rates with about 97% less prompt-to-response time. Benign accuracy stays at 98%. They draw no conclusion about shallow or first-token safety.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates jailbreak transferability and a draft-model safeguard; it does not use the fine-tuning or per-token-KL recipes in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Transferability varies with source LLM, draft SLM, jailbreak-generation method, optimization iteration, intent category, and response count. In safeguard evaluation, aggregation threshold also changes DFR and benign accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Jailbreak prompts optimised on Llama-3-70B, Qwen1.5-72B or Phi-3-medium transfer to small draft models. GCG transfers at up to 0.88 (Phi-3→SmolLM-135M, b=1). AutoDAN peaks at 0.53 and is mostly below 0.2. Transfer is low for SmolLM2 models and varies by intent category. Benign prompts yield near-zero unsafe ratios.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak prompts optimised for large aligned LLMs elicit unsafe outputs from small language models at rates depending on attack method, model pair and intent category.

record.problems: The transferability plots include confidence intervals, but the main text gives few exact pairwise rates. The reported transfer results depend on the safety classifier and the selected prompt sets; the paper does not test the first-token mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: Pairwise transferability heatmap entries, iteration trends, intent-category rates, and response-count curves are presented mainly in figures; their flattened layout does not support reliable assignment of every value to a specific model pair or condition. Safeguard DFR, latency, and benign-accuracy results are omitted because they assess the proposed guard rather than a claim version.

untested.parts: Per-token KL between aligned and base models; not measured.

Prefilling, suffix and decoding attacks on safety-trained models compared with unattacked harmful prompts. GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR prompts are generated, but their success on the aligned targets is not reported as a rate against a no-attack control.
Parameter localization of safety; not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 labels are dropped. The rows measure transfer to mostly non-safety-trained small models against a benign-prompt baseline, so they cannot show safety being bypassed. The defence DFR and latency results are correctly excluded as evaluations of the study's own method.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and refusal after fine-tuning.
Benign-data fine-tuning and harmful compliance after fine-tuning.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Compliant-opening prefills and decoding changes; the study tests jailbreak prompts, including GCG attacks, but does not isolate the effect of getting past initial response tokens.
Localization of safety behaviour in weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training to deepen safety and its robustness.

rows.subject: SmolLM-135M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated responses to GCG-generated jailbreak prompts crafted for Llama-3-70B; generated 20 draft responses per prompt and classified them with LlamaGuard-2-8B.
rows.baseline: Benign prompts cluster tightly around an unsafe ratio of 0.0.
rows.value: Malicious prompts show a long-tail distribution with non-zero unsafe response ratios; exact ratio values not stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors describe this specific Llama-3-70B/SmolLM-135M pair as having some attacks at ratio 0 and a significant density across (0.0, 1.0]. This measures jailbreak-prompt effects, not a compliant prefill or a comparison of suffix versus no suffix.
rows.check: SmolLM-135M is a small model with no stated safety training, so its unsafe outputs do not show a refusal being bypassed. The baseline is benign Just-Eval prompts, not the same harmful intents without the GCG suffix, so the attack's effect on refusal cannot be read. The row measures large-to-small jailbreak transfer and benign/malicious distinguishability, not V4.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2.1 and Figure 4: 20 responses per prompt, LlamaGuard-2-8B classification, Just-Eval benign baseline, and Llama-3-70B/SmolLM-135M example.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.locator_found: Section 5.2.1 and Figure 4: 20 responses per prompt, LlamaGuard-2-8B classification, Just-Eval benign baseline, and Llama-3-70B/SmolLM-135M example.

relation.reason: It cites harmful fine-tuning work as background but neither tests nor uses the shallow-safety finding.

tranche.reason: The study measures jailbreak transferability and safeguard performance, without establishing that the small draft models have safety-trained refusals being bypassed or testing another claim version.

source_check.notes: The statement's numerical results are supported by Appendix C, Figure 2 (b=1), rather than cited row R1, which concerns Figure 4 distributions. R1 compares malicious and benign prompts; it does not establish bypass of a safety-trained refusal.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GCG jailbreak prompts generated for Llama-3-70B and evaluated on SmolLM-135M
reader_labels.reason: The reported unsafe-response-ratio distribution has a non-zero long tail for malicious prompts relative to benign prompts (R1). This supports jailbreak effectiveness in this tested setting, not the proposed first-token mechanism.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transferability across attack methods and model pairs
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that transferability varies: GCG is more generalizable, while AutoDAN has lower and more fluctuating transferability, with some source-model pairs showing almost zero transfer (pairwise rates are not extracted here).
